newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish booming economic growth seen continuing - OECD.
newsitem.headline: Irish booming economic growth seen continuing - OECD.

text.p: Ireland's economy is expected to continue to expand rapidly over the next two years, although at a slower pace than in the past three years, the OECD said.

It said the Irish economy will continue to grow by more than 5.5 percent until the year 2000 and that the strong expansion in the past three years had boosted the real level of activity by almost one-fourth, more than three times the average increase in the rest of Europe.

"Against this background, the economy should continue to expand rapidly over the next two years," the OECD said. Its survey was due for release on Wednesday but sections of it were published early by local media.
It noted a rebound in the export sector in the second half of 1996 and a recovery underway in the computer industry.
The OECD expected private consumption to remain strong, "especially as the scrapping scheme for old cars based on tax incentives is to be prolonged until the end of 1997".
It said the boom in the housing sector may encourage some increase in residential property investment and added that the recent fall in long-term interest rates may stimulate business investment.

The OECD added, however, that further acceleration in growth, above that currently forecast for the next two years, could become a problem for the economy as it is already running at, or possibly above, its potential.
It said some signs of strain were already evident in the residential real estate market with the price of second-hand homes up 18 percent in the year to September 1996.
The OECD advised monetary authorities to be prepared to err on the side of caution and to tighten policy before markets become concerned about possible inflationary tensions.
"Such tightening would tend to dampen the demand for credit and, in turn, lessen the pressures in the real estate market," it said.
However, the scope to raise interest rates may be constrained by the need to maintain a stable exchange rate in the run-up to EMU, it added.
Fiscal policy should support monetary policy in keeping inflation low, it said, adding that the key was to restrain the growth in public expenditure.

"For the last two years the government has overshot its target of limiting the increase in spending to two percent above the rate of inflation. This objective has been extended to 1998 and 1999, despite continuing pressures on public-sector wages," it said.

The OECD recommended a contingency reserve, included in the government's three-year plan, should be used to cushion any revenue shortfalls in the event of an economic slowdown rather than to finance additional expenditure.

It recommended continued tax reduction saying the government will have to make cuts in 1998 and 1999 budgets in order to meet tax promises of Partnership 2000, a programme on work and competitiveness agreed between the authorities, employers and trade unions.
The OECD recommended reductions in corporate tax rates and a reduction in the high marginal tax rates and welfare benefit withdrawal rates faced by many low-paid workers.
